section_text: Data Fiduciary means any person who alone or in conjunction with other persons determines the purpose and means of processing of personal data.

Data Principal means the individual to whom the personal data relates and where such individual is a child includes the parents or lawful guardian of such child, and a person with disability includes her lawful guardian acting on her behalf.
Data Processor means any person who processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.

A person may process the personal data of a Data Principal only in accordance with the provisions of this Act and for a lawful purpose — (a) for which the Data Principal has given her consent; or (b) for certain legitimate uses as set out in section 7. Processing not in accordance with this Act is an offence punishable under the Schedule.

section_title: Notice before collection of personal data
section_text: Every request made to a Data Principal for consent shall be accompanied by or preceded by a notice given by the Data Fiduciary containing — (i) a description of personal data being collected and the purpose of processing; (ii) the manner in which the Data Principal may exercise her rights under section 16; (iii) the manner in which the Data Principal may make a complaint to the Board. Notice must be in clear and plain language, with itemised description of data sought. If consent obtained before commencement of Act, notice to be given as soon as reasonably practicable.

Consent given by the Data Principal shall be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action, and shall signify an agreement to the processing of her personal data for the specified purpose and limited to such personal data as is necessary for such specified purpose. Consent shall not be valid if it is bundled with consent for purposes not necessary. Data Principal may withdraw consent at any time with ease comparable to giving consent. Withdrawal of consent shall not affect lawfulness of processing before withdrawal.
amendment_note: Critical: no bundled consent allowed; withdrawal must be as easy as giving

section_text: A Data Fiduciary may process personal data of a Data Principal for any of the following uses without consent — (a) specified purpose for which Data Principal voluntarily provided data and has not indicated she does not consent; (b) State or its instrumentality providing benefit, service, certificate, licence or permit; (c) medical emergency involving threat to life or immediate threat to health; (d) measures during disaster/breakdown of public order for safety; (e) employment purpose — recruitment, termination, attendance, assessment, etc; (f) public interest including merger/demerger/insolvency, network/information security, credit scoring, recovery of debt, fraud prevention, whistleblowing.
amendment_note: NO general legitimate interest ground like GDPR Art 6(1)(f) — this is exhaustive list

section_text: (1) Data Fiduciary shall make reasonable efforts to ensure completeness, accuracy and consistency of personal data where such processing is likely to affect interests of Data Principal. (2) Data Fiduciary shall build reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach including encryption, access controls, de-identification, monitoring. (3) In the event of personal data breach, Data Fiduciary shall give notice to the Board and each affected Data Principal in prescribed form and manner. (4) When purpose fulfilled or Data Principal withdraws consent, Data Fiduciary shall erase personal data unless retention required by law. (5) Data Fiduciary shall publish business contact information of Data Protection Officer or person to answer questions regarding processing.
amendment_note: Breach notification to Board AND affected principals is mandatory

section_title: Additional obligations of Significant Data Fiduciary
section_text: Central Government may notify any Data Fiduciary or class of Data Fiduciaries as Significant Data Fiduciary (SDF) having regard to — volume and sensitivity of personal data processed; risk to rights of Data Principal; potential impact on sovereignty and integrity of India; risk to electoral democracy; security of State; public order. SDF shall — (a) appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India who represents SDF before Board; (b) appoint an independent data auditor to evaluate compliance; (c) undertake periodic Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA); (d) undertake periodic audit; (e) undertake such other measures as may be prescribed.
amendment_note: DPO mandatory only for SDFs, not all fiduciaries — key difference from GDPR

section_text: Before processing any personal data of a child, the Data Fiduciary shall obtain verifiable consent of the parent or lawful guardian of such child. Data Fiduciary shall not undertake such processing of personal data that is likely to cause any detrimental effect on the well-being of a child. Data Fiduciary shall not undertake tracking or behavioural monitoring of children or targeted advertising directed at children. Child means individual who has not completed eighteen years of age. Central Government may exempt certain classes of Data Fiduciaries from verifiable parental consent requirement if processing is verifiably safe.
amendment_note: Blanket ban on tracking/behavioural monitoring of children — no exception

section_text: A Data Principal may give, manage, review or withdraw her consent to the Data Fiduciary through a Consent Manager. Every Consent Manager shall be registered with the Board and shall be accountable to the Data Principal and shall act on behalf of the Data Principal. Board shall register Consent Managers subject to such conditions as prescribed including technical, operational and financial capacity. Consent Manager must be interoperable with other Consent Managers.

Data Principal shall have the right to — (a) obtain from Data Fiduciary a summary of personal data being processed and the processing activities undertaken by that Data Fiduciary with respect to such data, including identities of all other Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors with whom personal data has been shared, along with description of shared data; (b) correction and erasure of personal data; (c) grievance redressal; (d) nominate any other individual who shall exercise rights of the Data Principal in event of death or incapacity. No right to data portability in current Act.
amendment_note: NO right to portability — key gap vs GDPR

section_title: Right to grievance redressal and complaint to Board
section_text: Data Principal who has a grievance regarding action or inaction of Data Fiduciary may make a complaint to Data Fiduciary. If response not received within prescribed period or not satisfied with response, Data Principal may make complaint to Board. Board may on receipt of complaint and after giving opportunity of being heard, take such steps and pass such orders as it deems fit including directing Data Fiduciary to take necessary steps and imposing penalty under section 18.
amendment_note: Two-step: first to DF (prescribed period), then to Board

section_text: The Schedule specifies maximum penalties: (1) Failure to take reasonable security safeguards preventing breach — up to Rs. 250 crore; (2) Failure to notify Board and Data Principals of breach — up to Rs. 200 crore; (3) Non-fulfilment of children obligations — up to Rs. 200 crore; (4) Non-fulfilment of SDF obligations — up to Rs. 150 crore; (5) Breach of duties by Data Principal (false complaints, suppression) — up to Rs. 10,000; (6) Breach of any other provision — up to Rs. 50 crore. Board determines quantum considering nature, gravity, duration, type of data affected, repetitive nature, remedial steps taken, and gain/loss.
amendment_note: Highest penalty Rs. 250 crore — per breach, not per principal

section_text: Central Government may by notification exempt — (a) any instrumentality of the State processing personal data in interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of State, friendly relations with foreign States, maintenance of public order, preventing incitement to cognisable offence; (b) processing necessary for research, archiving or statistical purposes subject to prescribed standards; (c) a startup or other class of Data Fiduciaries. All exemptions must be just, fair, reasonable and proportionate in accordance with the Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1 proportionality framework.
amendment_note: Startup exemption power exists but not yet exercised; Puttaswamy proportionality test applies to all exemptions

section_title: Transfer of personal data outside India
section_text: The Data Fiduciary may transfer personal data of a Data Principal for processing to such country or territory outside India as may be notified by the Central Government. Central Government may restrict transfer to any country/territory by notification. Until such notification, transfer is permitted to all countries except those specifically restricted. No adequacy assessment required unlike GDPR — whitelist/blacklist model.
amendment_note: Blacklist model (not whitelist like GDPR) — all countries permitted unless specifically restricted
